reread_versions.relationship: parallel suffering of animals deprived of pasture
reread_versions.rationale: Joel's cattle weep because they lack pasture, and the sheep disappear. Jeremiah describes deer abandoning their young for lack of pasture and wild donkeys whose eyes fail because there is no grass. Both extend the land's calamity to animals, while the species and their responses differ.
reread_versions.source_text: What shall we store up for ourselves? Herds of cattle wept because they had no pasture, and flocks of sheep disappeared.

target_units.text: And deer in the field gave birth and abandoned their young, because there was no pasture.
Wild donkeys stood in wooded valleys; they drew in wind, their eyes failed, because there was no grass, because of a people of injustice.

reread_versions.relationship: repeated fire-and-flame imagery for devastation of the land
reread_versions.rationale: The cry to the Lord describes fire consuming the wilderness's beautiful places and flame kindling the field's trees. The advancing force is later preceded by consuming fire and followed by flame, leaving a desolate plain. The connection concerns the shared devastation imagery without specifying an unstated natural cause or identifying the force.
reread_versions.source_text: To Thee, Lord, I will cry, because fire consumed the beautiful places of the wilderness, and flame kindled all the field’s trees.

target_units.text: Before it is consuming fire, and behind it a kindled flame. The land before its face is like a garden of delight, and behind it a desolate plain; no one will escape it.

reread_versions.relationship: contrast between dried water outlets and God's provision of water for animals
reread_versions.rationale: Joel's animals look toward the Lord because water outlets have dried up. The psalm describes God sending springs through ravines to give drink to field beasts and wild donkeys, and watering the mountains. Both connect animal life with water under God's provision, while Joel describes its loss.
reread_versions.source_text: Even the animals of the plain looked up toward Thee, because outlets of water dried up, and fire devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness.

target_units.text: He sends springs into the ravines; waters will pass between the mountains.
They give drink to all the beasts of the field; wild donkeys will receive it for their thirst.
Upon them the birds of heaven will nest; from among the rocks they will give voice.
He waters mountains from His upper chambers; the earth will be filled with the fruit of Thy works.

reread_versions.relationship: parallel trumpet warnings associated with Zion and impending calamity
reread_versions.rationale: Joel commands a trumpet in Zion and an announcement on God's holy mountain because the Lord's day is present and near. Jeremiah commands a trumpet in the land and urgent flight to Zion because God brings calamity from the north. The warning signals and Zion connect the passages; Jeremiah explicitly directs flight.
reread_versions.source_text: Blow a trumpet in Zion! Proclaim on My holy mountain, and let all who inhabit the land be thrown into turmoil, because the Lord’s day is present; it is near,

target_units.text: Announce in Judah, and let it be heard in Jerusalem; say: Signal with a trumpet over the land, and cry loudly! Say: Gather, and let us enter the walled cities!
Take up and flee to Zion; hurry, do not stand still, for I am bringing evils from the north and great crushing.

reread_versions.relationship: close description of the day as darkness, gloom, cloud and mist
reread_versions.rationale: Joel describes a day of darkness and gloom, cloud and mist before depicting the numerous strong people. Zephaniah uses the same four atmospheric descriptions within its account of the Lord's day of wrath. This shared cluster concerns the day's character; Joel additionally compares the people's spread to dawn upon mountains.
reread_versions.source_text: a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist. Like dawn a numerous and strong people will be poured over the mountains. Its like has never existed, nor will another follow it through the years, for generations upon generations.

target_units.text: That day is a day of wrath, a day of affliction and constraint, a day of untimely ruin and destruction, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist,

reread_versions.relationship: reversal between a garden of delight and devastated land
reread_versions.rationale: Joel's advancing force leaves desolation where the land before it was like a garden of delight. Ezekiel's restoration makes devastated land like a garden of delight and restores the ruined cities. The same garden comparison marks opposite movements: devastation in Joel and renewal in Ezekiel.
reread_versions.source_text: Before it is consuming fire, and behind it a kindled flame. The land before its face is like a garden of delight, and behind it a desolate plain; no one will escape it.

target_units.text: They will say, “That devastated land has become like a garden of delight, and the deserted, devastated, razed cities stand fortified.”

reread_versions.relationship: parallel audible imagery of chariots in a scene of attack
reread_versions.rationale: Joel compares the leaping force's noise to chariots and to fire consuming stubble. Nahum describes the sounds of whips and shaking wheels, a pursuing horse and a jolting chariot. The connection is the sound and movement of chariots in battle imagery; Joel presents a comparison rather than naming actual chariots in the force.
reread_versions.source_text: With a sound like chariots they will leap upon mountain peaks, like the sound of a fiery flame devouring stubble, like a numerous and strong people arrayed for war.

target_units.text: The sound of whips and the sound of shaking wheels, of a pursuing horse and a jolting chariot,

reread_versions.relationship: shared image of faces like the scorching of a pot
reread_versions.rationale: Joel says the peoples are crushed before the force and every face is like the scorching of a pot. Nahum repeats this unusual facial image alongside broken hearts, loosening knees and bodily pangs. The specific pot comparison connects their portrayals of distress without substituting a different description of complexion.
reread_versions.source_text: Before it peoples will be crushed; every face is like the scorching of a pot.

target_units.text: Shaking out, tossing up and boiling over; broken hearts, loosening knees, pangs at every waist, and every face like the scorching of a pot.

reread_versions.relationship: related imagery of orderly collective advance
reread_versions.rationale: Joel's fighters run, climb walls and each proceeds on his own road without turning aside. Proverbs describes the kingless locust marching in good order at one command. The connection concerns disciplined collective movement; Proverbs explicitly names locusts, while this Joel unit describes the force through fighters and soldiers.
reread_versions.source_text: Like fighters they will run, and like soldiers they will climb the walls. Each will go on his own road, and they certainly will not turn aside from their paths,

target_units.text: the locust is without a king, yet marches out in good order at one command;

reread_versions.relationship: parallel destructive entry through windows
reread_versions.rationale: Joel's force climbs houses and enters through windows like thieves. Jeremiah personifies death as climbing through windows and entering the land to destroy children and young men. Both depict destructive entry through windows, while the entering force and the personified death remain distinct descriptions.
reread_versions.source_text: They will seize the city and run upon the walls; they will climb upon the houses and enter through windows like thieves.

target_units.text: For death climbed through your windows and entered your land, to wipe out little children outside and young men from the squares.

reread_versions.relationship: parallel darkening of sun, moon and stars within judgment
reread_versions.rationale: Joel describes the sun and moon growing dark and the stars sinking their brightness. Isaiah says the stars and their host will not give light, the rising sun will darken and the moon will not give its light. The coordinated loss of celestial light is shared; the surrounding oracles have their own settings.
reread_versions.source_text: Before them the earth will be thrown into turmoil and heaven shaken; the sun and moon will grow dark, and the stars will sink their brightness.

target_units.text: For heaven’s stars, Orion and all heaven’s array will not give light; it will grow dark as the sun rises, and the moon will not give its light.

reread_versions.relationship: close celestial darkening and shaking imagery in Jesus' discourse
reread_versions.rationale: Joel combines shaken heavens with darkened sun and moon and dimmed stars. Jesus' discourse likewise joins the sun's darkening, the moon's lost brightness, falling stars and shaken heavenly powers. The comparison preserves the difference between Joel's stars losing brightness and Matthew's stars falling.
reread_versions.source_text: Before them the earth will be thrown into turmoil and heaven shaken; the sun and moon will grow dark, and the stars will sink their brightness.

target_units.text: Immediately after the affliction of those days, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its brightness, the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

reread_versions.relationship: parallel question about enduring the day of divine manifestation
reread_versions.rationale: Joel describes the Lord's great and very manifest day and asks who will be sufficient for it. Malachi asks who will endure the day of entrance or stand at the appearance, then compares the coming one to a smelting fire. Both question human capacity before the day; their surrounding images differ.
reread_versions.source_text: The Lord will give His voice before His force, because His camp is very large, because the works of His words are strong. For the Lord’s day is great, great and very manifest; who will be sufficient for it?

target_units.text: And who will endure the day of his entrance? Or who will stand at his appearance? For he enters like a smelting fire and like launderers’ herb.

reread_versions.relationship: close summons to return to the Lord with the whole heart
reread_versions.rationale: Joel calls for return to God with the whole heart, accompanied by fasting, weeping and mourning. Deuteronomy speaks of returning to the Lord and obeying His voice with all heart and soul. The shared wholehearted return connects them; Joel specifies penitential actions while Deuteronomy emphasizes obedience.
reread_versions.source_text: “And now,” says the Lord your God, “turn to Me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning.”

target_units.text: and you return unto the Lord your God, and obey His voice according to all that I command you this day, with all your heart and with all your soul,

reread_versions.relationship: shared proclamation of God's compassion, mercy and patience
reread_versions.rationale: Joel grounds the return to God in His mercy, compassion, patience and abundant mercy. The proclamation before Moses describes the Lord as compassionate, merciful, slow to anger and abundant in mercy. These shared attributes support Joel's appeal; Joel additionally speaks here of relenting concerning calamities.
reread_versions.source_text: Tear your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because He is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and relents concerning calamities.

target_units.text: The Lord passed before him and proclaimed, “The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, slow to anger, abundant in mercy and true,

reread_versions.relationship: close shared description of mercy and relenting concerning calamities
reread_versions.rationale: Joel's invitation to return invokes God's mercy, compassion, patience, abundant mercy and relenting concerning calamities. Jonah acknowledges the same attributes in his prayer after Nineveh is spared. The shared description serves different responses: Joel encourages return, while Jonah's prayer occurs amid his grief over the outcome.
reread_versions.source_text: Tear your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because He is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and relents concerning calamities.

target_units.text: He prayed to the Lord and said, “O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I was quick to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that Thou art merciful and compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy, and relenting concerning calamities.

reread_versions.relationship: shared question of hope that God may turn and relent
reread_versions.rationale: Both passages ask who knows whether God will turn and relent. Joel hopes for a blessing that leaves sacrifice and drink offering; the Jonah passage hopes that God's fierce anger will turn so the people do not perish. Their common hopeful question does not state the same hoped-for result.
reread_versions.source_text: Who knows whether He will turn and relent and leave a blessing behind Him, a sacrifice and drink offering for the Lord our God?

target_units.text: “Who knows whether God will relent and turn from His fierce anger, so that we certainly do not perish?”

reread_versions.relationship: same-chapter repeated trumpet command in Zion with a different immediate purpose
reread_versions.rationale: Both units command sounding a trumpet in Zion. The opening command warns of the Lord's near day and the inhabitants' turmoil; this command joins the trumpet to consecrating a fast and proclaiming a service. The repeated signal links warning with the summoned response.
reread_versions.source_text: Blow a trumpet in Zion! Consecrate a fast; proclaim a service.

target_units.text: Blow a trumpet in Zion! Proclaim on My holy mountain, and let all who inhabit the land be thrown into turmoil, because the Lord’s day is present; it is near,

reread_versions.relationship: parallel comprehensive gathering explicitly including children
reread_versions.rationale: Joel gathers the people, elders, infants and nursing children, even calling bridegroom and bride from their chambers. Deuteronomy gathers men, women, children and sojourners to hear and obey the law. Both make young participants explicit in a communal gathering, while its occasion and the additional named groups differ.
reread_versions.source_text: Gather the people; consecrate the congregation. Choose elders; gather infants nursing at breasts. Let the bridegroom leave his bedroom and the bride her bridal chamber.

target_units.text: Gather the people, the men, and the women, and the children, and the sojourner who is in your cities, that they may hear, and that they may learn to fear the Lord your God; and they shall hearken to do all the words of this law.

reread_versions.relationship: shared plea for divine rescue against the nations' taunt
reread_versions.rationale: Joel's priests ask God to spare His people and prevent the nations from asking where their God is. The psalm asks for rescue and forgiveness for God's name, lest the nations voice the same question. Both connect mercy for the people with the challenge to God's name among the nations.
reread_versions.source_text: In the midst of the altar’s platform the priests who minister to the Lord will weep and say, “Spare Thy people, Lord, and do not give Thine inheritance to reproach, for nations to rule over them, so that they do not say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”

target_units.text: Help us, God our Savior. For the glory of Thy name, Lord, rescue us, and be propitious toward our sins for Thy name’s sake,
lest the nations say, “Where is their God?” And let vengeance for the poured-out blood of Thy servants be known among the nations before our eyes.

reread_versions.relationship: parallel divine jealousy associated with care for the chosen land or city
reread_versions.rationale: Joel says the Lord was jealous for His land and spared His people. Zechariah announces His great jealousy for Jerusalem and Zion, followed by His return to dwell there. Both place divine jealousy alongside renewed care, without making the target repeat Joel's specific statement of sparing.
reread_versions.source_text: Then the Lord became jealous for His land and spared His people.

target_units.text: “Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy; with great wrath I have been jealous for her.
Thus says the Lord: I will return to Zion and dwell within Jerusalem. Jerusalem will be called the True City, and the mountain of the Lord Almighty a Holy Mountain.

reread_versions.relationship: parallel promised grain, wine and oil with being filled
reread_versions.rationale: Joel promises God will send grain, wine and oil so the people are filled. Deuteronomy promises seasonal rain, the gathering of grain, wine and oil, and eating to fullness. The shared three staples and fullness connect the provisions; Joel also promises removal of reproach among the nations.
reread_versions.source_text: The Lord answered His people: “Look, I am sending out to you grain, wine and oil, and you will be filled with them. I will no longer give you over to reproach among the nations,

target_units.text: He shall give the rain unto your land in its season, the early and the latter rain; and you shall gather in your grain, and your wine, and your oil.
And He shall give grass in your fields for your cattle; and when you have eaten and are filled,

reread_versions.relationship: parallel rising stench within scenes of judgment
reread_versions.rationale: Joel describes the expelled northern one's decay and stench rising. Isaiah describes the odor rising from the wounded and dead under the Lord's judgment. Both portray judgment through an ascending offensive smell; the comparison does not identify the northern one with Isaiah's nations or rename Joel's first and last seas.
reread_versions.source_text: and I will drive away from you the one from the north and thrust it into a waterless land. I will make its front disappear into the first sea and its rear into the last sea; its decay will rise, and its stench will rise, because it magnified its deeds.”

target_units.text: Their wounded and dead will be thrown out; their odor will rise, and mountains will be soaked with their blood.

reread_versions.relationship: shared gladness because the Lord has done great things
reread_versions.rationale: Joel calls the land to courage and rejoicing because the Lord has done great things. The psalm reports joy and gladness with the same declaration of the Lord's great deeds. The common reason for joy is explicit, while Joel addresses the land and the psalm speaks of what God has done with His people.
reread_versions.source_text: Take courage, land! Rejoice and be glad, because the Lord has done great things.

target_units.text: Then our mouth was filled with joy and our tongue with exultation. Then they will say among the nations, “The Lord has done great things with them.”
The Lord has done great things with us; we became glad.

reread_versions.relationship: paired loss and restoration of pasture for animals
reread_versions.rationale: The earlier lament describes cattle without pasture and the disappearance of sheep. The reassurance tells the animals to take courage because the wilderness plains have sprouted, then describes fruitfulness. The renewed growth answers the earlier lack of pasture without assuming every named animal group is identical.
reread_versions.source_text: Take courage, animals of the plain, because the wilderness plains have sprouted, because a tree bore its fruit; vine and fig tree have given their strength.

target_units.text: What shall we store up for ourselves? Herds of cattle wept because they had no pasture, and flocks of sheep disappeared.

reread_versions.relationship: shared gift of early and latter rain
reread_versions.rationale: Joel says God has sent early and latter rain as before. Deuteronomy promises rain in season, specifically early and latter rain, together with gathered crops. The rain pair is the particular connection; Joel's separate phrase about food for righteousness is not replaced with a different rendering.
reread_versions.source_text: Children of Zion, rejoice and be glad in the Lord your God, because He gave you food for righteousness, and He will rain upon you early and late rainfall as before.

target_units.text: He shall give the rain unto your land in its season, the early and the latter rain; and you shall gather in your grain, and your wine, and your oil.

reread_versions.relationship: parallel abundance of grain and overflowing wine containers
reread_versions.rationale: Joel promises threshing floors filled with grain and winepresses overflowing with wine and oil. Proverbs promises storerooms full of grain and vats gushing with wine. The paired abundance of grain and wine connects the promises, while the storage places and Joel's added oil differ.
reread_versions.source_text: Threshing floors will be filled with grain, and winepresses will overflow with wine and oil.

target_units.text: so that your storerooms may be filled with an abundance of grain and your vats gush with wine.

reread_versions.relationship: repeated four destructive agents within a promise of repayment
reread_versions.rationale: The repayment promise names the same four destructive agents as the opening account, in a different order. The earlier unit describes each consuming the remainder left by another; this one identifies them as God's great force and promises repayment of the years they consumed.
reread_versions.source_text: “I will repay you for the years the locust devoured, the bruchus locust, the blight and the caterpillar—My great force that I sent among you.

target_units.text: What the caterpillar left, the locust devoured; what the locust left, the bruchus locust devoured; what the bruchus locust left, the blight devoured.

reread_versions.relationship: close sequence of eating to fullness and blessing or praising God
reread_versions.rationale: Joel promises abundant eating and fullness followed by praise of the Lord's name for His wonders. Deuteronomy commands eating to fullness and blessing the Lord for the good land He gave. Both connect satisfied eating with grateful acknowledgment of God; Joel additionally promises freedom from shame.
reread_versions.source_text: You will eat abundantly and be filled, and praise the name of the Lord your God for the wonders He has done with you. My people will certainly never be put to shame,

target_units.text: And you shall eat and be filled, and bless the Lord your God upon the good land which He has given you.

reread_versions.relationship: shared recognition that the Lord is God and there is no other
reread_versions.rationale: Joel promises recognition of God's presence among Israel and that He is their God with none beside Him. Deuteronomy describes the purpose of God's acts as knowing that the Lord is God and none is beside Him. The explicit recognition and exclusive divine identity connect the passages within different accounts of God's acts.
reread_versions.source_text: and you will recognize that I am in Israel’s midst, that I am the Lord your God and there is no other besides Me. All My people will certainly never again be put to shame.”

target_units.text: That you might know that the Lord your God, He is God, and there is none beside Him.

reread_versions.relationship: explicit quotation of Joel's promise to pour out the Spirit
reread_versions.rationale: Peter expressly introduces the prophet Joel and quotes the Spirit poured upon all flesh, sons and daughters prophesying, young men seeing visions and elders dreaming. Joel says after these things, while Acts frames the quotation as in the last days; the named groups and gifts closely correspond.
reread_versions.source_text: “And it shall be after these things, that I will pour out of My Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your elders shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions.

target_units.text: ‘In the last days, God says, I will pour out of My Spirit upon all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy; your young men will see visions, and your elders will dream dreams.

reread_versions.relationship: explicit quotation extending the Spirit's gift to male and female slaves
reread_versions.rationale: Peter's quotation retains the promise of pouring out the Spirit upon both male and female slaves in those days. Acts also explicitly says they will prophesy in this unit. The shared inclusion of both slave groups is particular, while Joel's source unit here states the pouring out of the Spirit.
reread_versions.source_text: Even upon male slaves and female slaves in those days I will pour out of My Spirit.

target_units.text: Even upon My male slaves and My female slaves in those days I will pour out of My Spirit, and they will prophesy.

reread_versions.relationship: explicit quotation of wonders involving blood, fire and smoke
reread_versions.rationale: Joel promises wonders in heaven and on earth, naming blood, fire and vapor of smoke. Acts quotes the corresponding wonders and signs with blood, fire and a cloud of smoke. The three phenomena and heavenly and earthly scope connect them, with their supplied descriptions of smoke preserved.
reread_versions.source_text: I will give wonders in heaven and upon the earth: blood, fire and a vapor of smoke.

target_units.text: I will give wonders in heaven above and signs on the earth below: blood and fire and a cloud of smoke.

reread_versions.relationship: explicit quotation of the sun and moon signs before the Lord's day
reread_versions.rationale: Both passages say the sun will change into darkness and the moon into blood before the Lord's great and manifest day. Acts includes this wording within Peter's explicitly introduced quotation of Joel. The close correspondence concerns both signs and their timing before the day.
reread_versions.source_text: The sun will turn to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the Lord’s great and manifest day.

target_units.text: The sun will be changed into darkness and the moon into blood before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes.

reread_versions.relationship: explicit quotation of salvation for everyone calling on the Lord's name
reread_versions.rationale: Acts repeats Joel's declaration that everyone calling upon the Lord's name will be saved. This quoted unit stops with that declaration; Joel's source unit continues with escape in Zion and Jerusalem and bearers of good news whom the Lord called. The retained connection is the shared salvation statement.
reread_versions.source_text: Everyone who calls upon the Lord’s name will be saved, for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be one who escapes, as the Lord said, and bearers of good news whom the Lord has called.”

target_units.text: And everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.’

reread_versions.relationship: quoted salvation promise applied to Jew and Greek
reread_versions.rationale: Romans repeats the declaration that everyone calling upon the Lord's name will be saved and places it beside the statement that Jew and Greek share the same Lord. Joel's everyone supplies the matching salvation wording, while Romans explicitly names these two groups in its application.
reread_versions.source_text: Everyone who calls upon the Lord’s name will be saved, for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be one who escapes, as the Lord said, and bearers of good news whom the Lord has called.”

target_units.text: For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord is Lord of all, being rich toward all who call upon Him;
for “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.”

reread_versions.relationship: shared reversal of captivity associated with Judah's holy city
reread_versions.rationale: Joel announces the turning back of Judah and Jerusalem's captivity. The psalm remembers the Lord turning back Zion's captivity and then petitions Him to turn back captivity again. The common reversal of captivity connects promise, remembrance and renewed prayer without making their temporal settings identical.
reread_versions.source_text: “For look, in those days and at that time, when I turn back the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem,

target_units.text: A song of the ascents. When the Lord turned back Zion’s captivity, we became like those comforted.
Then our mouth was filled with joy and our tongue with exultation. Then they will say among the nations, “The Lord has done great things with them.”
The Lord has done great things with us; we became glad.
Turn back our captivity, Lord, like torrents in the south.

reread_versions.relationship: parallel judgment on nations for appropriating God's land
reread_versions.rationale: Joel gathers nations for judgment over His scattered people and the division of His land. Ezekiel announces wrath against nations and Idumea because they gave His land to themselves as a possession. Both ground judgment in God's claim upon the land; Ezekiel additionally names Idumea among the offenders.
reread_versions.source_text: I will gather all the nations and bring them down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. There I will enter into judgment with them over My people and My inheritance Israel, who were scattered among the nations; and they divided up My land

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord, the Lord: Surely in the fire of My wrath I have spoken against the remaining nations and all Idumea, because they gave My land to themselves as a possession with rejoicing, dishonoring lives so as to destroy through plunder.

Therefore prophesy over Israel’s land and say to the mountains, hills, ravines and valleys, Thus says the Lord: Behold, I have spoken in My jealousy and My wrath because you bore the nations’ reproaches.
Therefore I will raise My hand against the nations around you; these will receive their own dishonor.

reread_versions.relationship: related trading of captive people for payment
reread_versions.rationale: Joel describes lots cast over God's people and exchanges of boys for prostitutes and girls for wine. Nicanor plans to sell Jewish captives to discharge royal tribute and invites buyers at a stated price. Both treat captive people as commodities, while Joel reports exchanges and Maccabees describes a proposed sale.
reread_versions.source_text: and cast lots over My people; they gave the boys to prostitutes and sold the girls for wine, which they drank.

target_units.text: Nicanor determined to discharge the king’s tribute to the Romans, amounting to two thousand talents, from the captivity of the Jews.

He immediately sent to the coastal cities, inviting people to buy Jewish bodies and promising to give ninety bodies for a talent, not expecting the judgment that was about to follow upon him from the Almighty.

reread_versions.relationship: close formula of recompense repaid upon the offender's head
reread_versions.rationale: Joel threatens Tyre, Sidon and the Galilee of foreigners with swift repayment of their recompense upon their heads. Obadiah says the addressee will receive according to his deeds and his recompense will be repaid upon his own head. The matching repayment formula connects distinct addressed offenders.
reread_versions.source_text: What have you to do with Me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of foreigners? Are you repaying Me a recompense? Or do you bear a sharp grudge against Me? I will speedily repay your recompense upon your heads,

target_units.text: For the day of the Lord is near against all the nations. Just as you acted, so it will be for you; your recompense will be repaid upon your own head.

reread_versions.relationship: parallel removal of the Lord's valuables into a foreign temple
reread_versions.rationale: Joel accuses the addressed peoples of taking God's silver, gold and chosen beautiful things into their temples. Daniel reports part of the Lord's sacred vessels carried to Babylon and deposited in the king's idol-temple. Both concern sacred property transferred into foreign worship places, without identifying the seizures as one event.
reread_versions.source_text: because you took My silver and gold and brought My chosen and beautiful things into your temples,

target_units.text: The Lord handed the city into his hands, together with Joakim king of Judea and a portion of the Lord’s sacred vessels. He carried them away to Babylon and deposited them in his idol-temple.

reread_versions.relationship: related accusation of Tyre's participation in transferring captives
reread_versions.rationale: Joel's address to Tyre and the other named regions condemns selling sons of Judah and Jerusalem to sons of the Greeks. Amos accuses Tyre of confining Solomon's captives in Idumea and forgetting a covenant of brothers. The shared charge concerns captive transfer; the supplied captive descriptions and destinations differ.
reread_versions.source_text: and sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, so as to thrust them out of their own borders.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn away from her, because they shut Solomon’s captives up in Idumea and did not remember a covenant of brothers.

reread_versions.relationship: repeated formula of recompense returned upon the offender's head
reread_versions.rationale: Joel joins the rousing of sold people with repayment of recompense upon the captors' heads. Obadiah likewise promises repayment upon the offender's own head according to his deeds. The particular verbal connection is the repayment formula; Obadiah's target unit does not itself describe rousing sold captives.
reread_versions.source_text: Look, I am rousing them from the place to which you sold them, and I will repay your recompense upon your heads,

target_units.text: For the day of the Lord is near against all the nations. Just as you acted, so it will be for you; your recompense will be repaid upon your own head.

reread_versions.relationship: same-chapter reversal of captive trading
reread_versions.rationale: The earlier accusation names sons of Judah and Jerusalem sold away from their borders. The judgment now places the offenders' sons and daughters into the hands of Judah's sons and onward into captivity to a distant nation. The reversal concerns whose families are transferred and Judah's changed role.
reread_versions.source_text: and I will sell your sons and daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah, and they will sell them into captivity to a nation far away, because the Lord has spoken.”

target_units.text: and sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, so as to thrust them out of their own borders.

reread_versions.relationship: parallel commands to prepare for war and go up to attack
reread_versions.rationale: Joel addresses the nations with a call to consecrate war, rouse fighters and bring warriors forward. Jeremiah commands preparation for war and rising to go up against the city, by noon and by night. Both summon forces to military action, with Jeremiah supplying particular times and an attack on Jerusalem in its context.
reread_versions.source_text: Proclaim these things among the nations: Consecrate war! Rouse the fighters! Draw near and come up, all soldiers!

target_units.text: Prepare yourselves for war against her! Rise, and let us go up against her at noon! Woe to us, because the day has declined, because evening’s shadows are failing!
Rise, and let us go up in the night and destroy her foundations!

reread_versions.relationship: opposite transformations of agricultural tools and weapons
reread_versions.rationale: Joel commands turning plows into swords and sickles into lances for mobilization. Isaiah promises swords beaten into plows and spears into sickles when nations cease learning war. The agricultural and military objects move in opposite directions, marking the contrast between preparation for battle and the end of war.
reread_versions.source_text: Beat your plows into swords and your sickles into lances; let the powerless say, “I am strong!”

target_units.text: He will judge between the nations and reprove a numerous people. They will beat their swords into plows and their spears into sickles. Nation will no longer take sword against nation, and they will certainly no longer learn to wage war.

reread_versions.relationship: same-chapter paired summons for the powerless or meek to become fighters
reread_versions.rationale: Joel first tells the powerless to say they are strong. The next summons gathers the surrounding nations and calls for the meek to become a fighter. The adjacent commands share the particular reversal from weakness or meekness to martial strength within the gathering for battle.
reread_versions.source_text: Assemble and enter, all surrounding nations, and gather there! Let the meek become a fighter!

target_units.text: Beat your plows into swords and your sickles into lances; let the powerless say, “I am strong!”

reread_versions.relationship: parallel gathering of nations before a seated judge
reread_versions.rationale: Joel says the Lord sits in the Valley of Jehoshaphat to judge all the nations round about. Matthew describes the Son of Man sitting on His glorious throne with all nations gathered before Him for separation. The gathering and seated judgment connect the scenes; the named setting and Joel's round-about qualification remain distinct.
reread_versions.source_text: Let all the nations be roused and come up to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, because there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.

target_units.text: When the Son of Man comes in His glory, and all the angels with Him, then He will sit upon the throne of His glory.
All the nations will be gathered before Him, and He will separate them from one another as the shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.

reread_versions.relationship: related winepress imagery for judgment on evil
reread_versions.rationale: Joel commands putting in sickles and treading the full winepress because evil has multiplied. Isaiah describes garments as from a trodden winepress, followed by trampling in wrath and blood brought to the earth. Both associate pressing and trampling with judgment, while the garments and explicit blood belong to Isaiah's description.
reread_versions.source_text: Send out sickles, because the vintage is at hand! Enter and tread, because the winepress is full; the vats overflow, because their evils have multiplied.

target_units.text: Why are Thy garments red and Thy clothes as though from a trodden winepress?
“I am full of what has been trodden. No man from the nations is with Me. I trampled them in wrath, crushed them like earth, and brought their blood down to earth.

reread_versions.relationship: repeated darkening of the sun, moon and stars
